nodes.name: k-colouring
nodes.statement: A {\em $k$-colouring} of a graph~$G=(V,E)$ is a mapping $c:V\to \{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$.

nodes.name: Colouring
nodes.statement: The {\sc Colouring} problem that of deciding whether a given graph~$G$ has a $k$-colouring for a given integer~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph G admits a k-colouring for given k.

nodes.name: k-Colouring (fixed k)
nodes.statement: If~$k$ is fixed, then we write $k$-{\sc Colouring} instead.

nodes.name: NP-completeness of 3-Colouring
nodes.statement: It is well known that even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete~\cite{Lo73}.
conclusions: even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete

nodes.name: hereditary graph class
nodes.statement: A class is hereditary if it closed under vertex deletion.

nodes.name: Colouring is polynomial for perfect graphs (Grötschel-Lovász-Schrijver)
nodes.statement: A classical result in the area is due to Gr\"otschel, Lov\'asz, and Schrijver~\cite{GLS84}, who showed that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs

nodes.name: H-free (set of forbidden graphs)
nodes.statement: Graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in a set~${\cal H}$ are said to be {\em ${\cal H}$-free}.
differentia: no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in a set~${\cal H}$

nodes.name: Hereditary classes are characterised by forbidden induced subgraphs
nodes.statement: It is readily seen that a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free.
conclusions: a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the minimal forbidden induced subgraph set
nodes.statement: If the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs, then~${\cal H}$ is unique.
assumptions: the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs
conclusions: ${\cal H}$ is unique

nodes.name: Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
nodes.statement: For example, the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes~\cite{CRST06}.
nodes.statement_short: The minimal forbidden induced subgraphs of perfect graphs are the odd holes and odd antiholes.
conclusions: the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes

nodes.name: Král'-Kratochvíl-Tuza-Woeginger dichotomy for H-free graphs
nodes.statement: Kr\'al', Kratochv\'{\i}l, Tuza, and Woeginger~\cite{KKTW01} classified the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for the case where~${\cal H}$ consists of a single graph~$H$. They proved that {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable if~$H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$ and {\sf NP}-complete otherwise.\footnote{We refer to Section~\ref{s-pre} for notation used throughout Section~\ref{s-intro}.}
nodes.statement_short: Colouring on H-free graphs is polynomial if H is an induced subgraph of P_4 or P_1+P_3, NP-complete otherwise.
assumptions: $H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable
{\sf NP}-complete otherwise

nodes.name: bigenic graph class
nodes.statement: Kr\'al' et al.~\cite{KKTW01} also initiated a complexity study of {\sc Colouring} for graph classes defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$. Such graph classes are said to be {\em bigenic}.
differentia: defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$

nodes.name: Open cases for Colouring with two forbidden graphs on at most four vertices
nodes.statement: For instance, if we forbid two graphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ with $|V(H_1)|\leq 4$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 4$, then there are three open cases left, namely when $(H_1,H_2)\in \{(K_{1,3},4P_1),\allowbreak (K_{1,3},2P_1+\nobreak P_2),\allowbreak (C_4,4P_1)\}$ (see~\cite{LM15} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fourvertices}).
nodes.statement_short: For two forbidden graphs on at most 4 vertices, only three cases of Colouring remain open.
assumptions: we forbid two graphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ with $|V(H_1)|\leq 4$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 4$
conclusions: there are three open cases left

nodes.name: Open cases for Colouring with two connected forbidden graphs on at most five vertices
nodes.statement: If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ are connected with $|V(H_1)|\leq 5$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 5$, then there are four open cases left, namely when $H_1=P_5$ and $H_2\in \{\overline{C_3+2P_1},\overline{C_3+P_2},\overline{P_1+2P_2}\}$ (see~\cite{KMP} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}) and when $H_1=K_{1,3}$ and $H_2=\overline{C_4+P_1}$ (see~\cite{ML17} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}).
nodes.statement_short: For two connected forbidden graphs on at most 5 vertices, four cases remain open (three with H_1=P_5, one with H_1=K_{1,3}).
conclusions: there are four open cases left

nodes.name: Colouring of (H, co-H)-free graphs (Blanché et al.)
nodes.statement: To give another example, Blanch\'e et al.~\cite{BDJP16} determined the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for $(H,\overline{H})$-free graphs for every graph~$H$ except when $H=P_3+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 3$ or $H=P_4+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 2$.
conclusions: determined the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for $(H,\overline{H})$-free graphs for every graph~$H$ except when $H=P_3+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 3$ or $H=P_4+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 2$

nodes.name: Precolouring Extension
nodes.statement: For the first problem, we are given a graph~$G$, an integer~$k$ and a $k$-colouring~$c'$ defined on an induced subgraph of~$G$. The question is whether~$G$ has a $k$-colouring~$c$ extending~$c'$.
nodes.statement_short: Given G, k and a k-colouring c' of an induced subgraph, decide whether c' extends to a k-colouring of G.

nodes.name: List Colouring
nodes.statement: For the second problem, each vertex~$u$ of the input graph~$G$ has a list~$L(u)$ of colours. Here the question is whether~$G$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$, that is, with $c(u)\in L(u)$ for all $u\in V(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Given lists L(u) of colours, decide whether G has a colouring with c(u) in L(u) for all u.

nodes.name: almost classified
nodes.statement: We say that a connected graph~$H_1$ is {\em almost classified} if {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or {\sf NP}-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$.
differentia: {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or {\sf NP}-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$

nodes.name: Which connected graphs are almost classified?
nodes.statement: This leads to the following research question: \begin{center} {\em Which connected graphs are almost classified?} \end{center}

nodes.name: Finite simple undirected graphs
nodes.statement: We consider only finite, undirected graphs without multiple edges or self-loops.

nodes.name: complement of a graph
nodes.statement: The {\em complement}~$\overline{G}$ of~$G$ is the graph with vertex set~$V(G)$ and an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$.
differentia: an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$

nodes.name: induced subgraph
nodes.statement: For a subset $S\subseteq V$, we let~$G[S]$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ {\em induced} by~$S$, which has vertex set~$S$ and edge set $\{uv\; |\; u,v\in S, uv\in E\}$.
differentia: edge set $\{uv\; |\; u,v\in S, uv\in E\}$

nodes.name: (H_1,...,H_p)-free graph
nodes.statement: A graph~$G$ is {\em $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free} if~$G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$.
differentia: $G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$

nodes.name: H_1-free shorthand
nodes.statement: If~$p=1$, we may write $H_1$-free instead of $(H_1)$-free.

nodes.name: disjoint union
nodes.statement: The {\em disjoint union} $G+\nobreak H$ of two vertex-disjoint graphs~$G$ and~$H$ is the graph $(V(G)\cup V(H), E(G)\cup E(H))$.

nodes.name: rG (r disjoint copies)
nodes.statement: The disjoint union of~$r$ copies of a graph~$G$ is denoted by~$rG$.

nodes.name: cycle, complete graph and path C_r, K_r, P_r
nodes.statement: The graphs~$C_r$, $K_r$ and~$P_r$ denote the cycle, complete graph and path on~$r$ vertices, respectively.

nodes.name: complete bipartite graph K_{r,s}
nodes.statement: The graph~$K_{r,s}$ denotes the complete bipartite graph with partition classes of size~$r$ and~$s$, respectively.

nodes.name: claw
nodes.statement: The graph~$K_{1,3}$ is also called the {\em claw}.

nodes.name: subdivided claw S_{h,i,j}
nodes.statement: The graph~$S_{h,i,j}$, for $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$, denotes the {\em subdivided claw}, that is, the tree that has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$ and exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively.
differentia: has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$ and exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively

nodes.name: graph T_{h,i,j}
nodes.statement:
The graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ with $0\leq h\leq i\leq j$ denotes the graph with vertices $a_0,\ldots,a_h$, $b_0,\ldots,b_i$ and $c_0,\ldots,c_j$ and edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_pa_{p+1}$ for $p \in \{0,\ldots, h-
obreak1\}$, $b_pb_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,i-
obreak 1\}$ and $c_pc_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,j-
obreak 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: T_{h,i,j}: a triangle a_0b_0c_0 with pendant paths of lengths h, i, j attached at its three vertices.

nodes.name: T_{h,i,j} is the line graph of S_{h+1,i+1,j+1}
nodes.statement: Also note that~$T_{h,i,j}$ is the line graph of~$S_{h+1,i+1,j+1}$.
conclusions: $T_{h,i,j}$ is the line graph of~$S_{h+1,i+1,j+1}$

nodes.name: class T
nodes.statement: Let~${\cal T}$ be the class of graphs every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$.
differentia: every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$

nodes.name: Schindl's theorem
nodes.statement: For $p\geq 1$, let $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$. Then {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs.
assumptions: let $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs

nodes.name: Finitely many open pairs avoiding the claw and P_5
nodes.statement: There are only finitely many pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$, such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown.
nodes.statement_short: Excluding K_{1,3} and P_5, only finitely many pairs of connected graphs (H_1,H_2) have open Colouring complexity.
conclusions: There are only finitely many pairs
such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown
nodes.label: t-almost1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem t-almost1
nodes.statement:
We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices. \medskip 
oindent Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases. \medskip 
oindent { f Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\ Then~$H_1$ is a path. First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+
obreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+
obreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs. Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant. \medskip 
oindent { f Case 2.} $H_1$ is a tree and not $K_{1,3}$-free, and~$H_2$ is $K_{1,3}$-free and not a tree.\ Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices. By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for the class of $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis using known hardness results to bound both H_1 and H_2. Ramsey's Theorem bounds |V(H_2)| once H_2 is shown K_6- (or K_4-) and 4P_1-free.

nodes.name: Observation and reduction to two cases
nodes.statement: We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices. \medskip \noindent Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Prove an observation about trees, then reduce to two cases using known hardness results.

nodes.name: Observation on trees
nodes.statement: We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Every tree other than K_{1,3}, P_5 and induced subgraphs of P_4 contains K_{1,4}, S_{1,1,2} or is a path on at least 6 vertices.

nodes.name: Observation on trees avoiding K_{1,3}, P_5 and P_4
nodes.statement: We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices.
assumptions: $H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$
conclusions: $H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices

nodes.name: Reduction via known hardness results
nodes.statement: Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Dismiss P_4-subgraph cases (polynomial) and cases where both contain cycles or claws (NP-complete), leaving two cases.

nodes.name: Case 1: H_1 a K_{1,3}-free tree
nodes.statement:
{ f Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\ Then~$H_1$ is a path. First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+
obreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+
obreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs. Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Case H_1 is a path; split on whether it has at least 22 vertices.

nodes.name: H_1 has at least 22 vertices
nodes.statement: First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+\nobreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+\nobreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs.
nodes.statement_short: Long path H_1: H_2 must be a tree, containing 4P_1 or 2P_1+P_2, giving NP-completeness.

nodes.name: H_1 has at most 21 vertices
nodes.statement: Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(2P_1+\nobreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Short path H_1: H_2 may be assumed (K_6,4P_1)-free, so Ramsey bounds |V(H_2)|.

nodes.name: Case 2: H_1 a tree with a claw, H_2 claw-free non-tree
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2.} $H_1$ is a tree and not $K_{1,3}$-free, and~$H_2$ is $K_{1,3}$-free and not a tree.\\ Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices. By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for the class of $(2P_1+\nobreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Bound H_1 by max degree and P_22-freeness, then bound H_2 by Ramsey.

nodes.name: Bound the size of H_1
nodes.statement: Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Hardness results force H_1 to be a P_22-free tree of max degree at most 4, hence bounded.

nodes.name: Bound the size of H_2
nodes.statement: By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for the class of $(2P_1+\nobreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.\qed
nodes.statement_short: H_2 may be assumed (K_4,4P_1)-free, so Ramsey's Theorem bounds |V(H_2)|.

nodes.name: Every connected graph except the claw and P_5 is almost classified
nodes.statement: Every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$ is almost classified.
assumptions: Every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$
conclusions: is almost classified
nodes.label: t-almost

nodes.name: List Colouring is NP-complete for complete split graphs
nodes.statement: As observed in~\cite{GP14}, a minor modification of this construction yields that {\sc List Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for complete split graphs, which are the graphs obtained from complete bipartite graphs by changing one of the bipartition classes into a clique.
conclusions: {\sc List Colouring} is {\sf NP}-complete for complete split graphs

nodes.name: Not-All-Equal 3-Satisfiability with positive literals only
nodes.statement: To define this problem, let $X= \{x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\}$ be a set of logical variables, and let ${\cal C} = \{C_1, C_2,\ldots, C_m\}$ be a set of $3$-literal clauses over~$X$ in which all literals are positive and every literal appears at most once in each clause. The question is whether~$X$ has a truth assignment such that each clause in~${\cal C}$ contains at least one true literal and at least one false literal.
nodes.statement_short: Given positive 3-literal clauses over X, find a truth assignment with each clause containing a true and a false literal.

nodes.name: satisfying truth assignment
nodes.statement: If so, we say that such a truth assignment is {\em satisfying}.

nodes.name: Golovach-Heggernes construction of (G_1, L)
nodes.statement:
Let $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only. We construct an instance $(G_1,L)$ of {\sc List Colouring} as follows. For each~$x_i$ we introduce a vertex, which we also denote by~$x_i$ and which we say is of {\em $x$-type}. We define $L(x_1)=\{1,2\}$, $L(x_2)=\{3,4\},\ldots,L(x_n)=\{2n-1,2n\}$. In this way, each~$x_i$ has one odd colour and one even colour in its list, and all lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint. For each~$C_j$ we introduce two vertices, which we denote by~$C_j$ and~$C_j'$ and which we say are of {\em $C$-type}. If $C_j=\{x_g,x_h,x_i\}$ with $L(x_g)=\{a,a+
obreak 1\}$, $L(x_h)=\{b,b+
obreak 1\}$ and $L(x_i)=\{c,c+
obreak 1\}$, then we set $L(C_j)=\{a,b,c\}$ and $L(C_j')=\{a+
obreak 1,b+
obreak 1,c+
obreak 1\}$. Hence each~$C_j$ has only odd colours in its list and each~$C_j'$ has only even colours in its list. To obtain the graph~$G_1$ we add an edge between every vertex of $x$-type and every vertex of $C$-type.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce positive NAE-3SAT to List Colouring on a complete bipartite graph: variable vertices with lists {2i-1,2i}, two clause vertices with odd/even colour lists, all variable-clause edges.
input: $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only

nodes.name: Variable vertices
nodes.statement: For each~$x_i$ we introduce a vertex, which we also denote by~$x_i$ and which we say is of {\em $x$-type}.
nodes.statement_short: Add one x-type vertex per variable.

nodes.name: Variable lists
nodes.statement: We define $L(x_1)=\{1,2\}$, $L(x_2)=\{3,4\},\ldots,L(x_n)=\{2n-1,2n\}$. In this way, each~$x_i$ has one odd colour and one even colour in its list, and all lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Give x_i the list {2i-1, 2i}.

nodes.name: Clause vertices
nodes.statement: For each~$C_j$ we introduce two vertices, which we denote by~$C_j$ and~$C_j'$ and which we say are of {\em $C$-type}.
nodes.statement_short: Add two C-type vertices C_j, C_j' per clause.

nodes.name: Clause lists
nodes.statement:
If $C_j=\{x_g,x_h,x_i\}$ with $L(x_g)=\{a,a+
obreak 1\}$, $L(x_h)=\{b,b+
obreak 1\}$ and $L(x_i)=\{c,c+
obreak 1\}$, then we set $L(C_j)=\{a,b,c\}$ and $L(C_j')=\{a+
obreak 1,b+
obreak 1,c+
obreak 1\}$. Hence each~$C_j$ has only odd colours in its list and each~$C_j'$ has only even colours in its list.
nodes.statement_short: C_j gets the odd colours and C_j' the even colours of its three variables.

nodes.name: Join variable and clause vertices
nodes.statement: To obtain the graph~$G_1$ we add an edge between every vertex of $x$-type and every vertex of $C$-type.
nodes.statement_short: Make G_1 complete bipartite between x-type and C-type vertices.

nodes.name: G_1 is complete bipartite
nodes.statement: Note that~$G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$.
conclusions: $G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$

nodes.name: instance (G_2, L)
nodes.statement: We also construct an instance $(G_2,L)$ where~$G_2$ is obtained from~$G_1$ by adding edges between every pair of vertices of $x$-type.

nodes.name: G_2 is a complete split graph
nodes.statement: Note that~$G_2$ is a complete split graph.
conclusions: $G_2$ is a complete split graph

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma l-true (by reference)
nodes.statement: The following lemma is straightforward. We refer to~\cite{GH09} for a proof for the case involving~$G_1$. The case involving~$G_2$ follows from this proof and the fact that the lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint, as observed in~\cite{GP14}.
nodes.statement_short: Pointer to the proof of [GH09] for G_1; the G_2 case follows since the lists L(x_i) are pairwise disjoint.

nodes.name: Golovach-Heggernes equivalence lemma
nodes.statement: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G_1$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G_2$ has a colouring that respects~$L$.
conclusions: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G_1$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G_2$ has a colouring that respects~$L$
nodes.label: l-true

nodes.name: graphs G'_1 and G'_2
nodes.statement: We now extend~$G_1$ and~$G_2$ into graphs~$G'_1$ and~$G'_2$, respectively, by adding a clique~$K$ consisting of~$2n$ new vertices $k_1,\ldots,k_{2n}$ and by adding an edge between a vertex~$k_\ell$ and a vertex~$u$ of the original graph if and only if $\ell\notin L(u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Add a clique on 2n new vertices k_l to G_1 (resp. G_2), joining k_l to u exactly when l is not in L(u).

nodes.name: k-type vertices
nodes.statement: We say that the vertices $k_1,\ldots,k_{2n}$ are of {\em $k$-type}.

nodes.name: Equivalence with 2n-colouring of G'_1 and G'_2
nodes.statement: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G'_1$ has a $2n$-colouring if and only if~$G'_2$ has a $2n$-colouring.
conclusions: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G'_1$ has a $2n$-colouring if and only if~$G'_2$ has a $2n$-colouring
nodes.label: l-truth

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma l-truth
nodes.statement: Let $i\in \{1,2\}$. By Lemma~\ref{l-true}, we only need to show that~$G_i$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring. First suppose that~$G_i$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$. We extend~$c$ to a colouring~$c'$ of~$G'_i$ by setting $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in\{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Now suppose that~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring~$c'$. As the $k$-type vertices form a clique, we may assume without loss of generality that $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in \{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Hence the restriction of~$c'$ to~$G_i$ yields a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to list colouring via Lemma l-true; extend by colouring k_l with l, and conversely normalise the clique colours.

nodes.name: Reduce to the list-colouring equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $i\in \{1,2\}$. By Lemma~\ref{l-true}, we only need to show that~$G_i$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma l-true it suffices to relate L-respecting colourings of G_i and 2n-colourings of G'_i.

nodes.name: List colouring gives 2n-colouring
nodes.statement: First suppose that~$G_i$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$. We extend~$c$ to a colouring~$c'$ of~$G'_i$ by setting $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in\{1,\ldots,2n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend c by colouring k_l with colour l.

nodes.name: 2n-colouring gives list colouring
nodes.statement: Now suppose that~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring~$c'$. As the $k$-type vertices form a clique, we may assume without loss of generality that $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in \{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Hence the restriction of~$c'$ to~$G_i$ yields a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Normalise colours on the clique K; the restriction to G_i respects L.

nodes.name: Forbidden induced subgraphs of G'_1
nodes.statement: The graph~$G_1'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free.
conclusions: The graph~$G_1'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free
nodes.label: l-s1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma l-s1
nodes.statement:
We will prove that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $(C_4,3P_2,T_{0,2,2})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_1'}$, the set of $x$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_1'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex. \medskip 
oindent { f $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$; say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_1'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of $x$-type vertices and the set of $C$-type vertices each from a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, but~$u_2$ is non-adjacent to~$u_4$, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_2$ is of $x$-type and~$u_4$ is of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_1'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $C_4$-free. \medskip 
oindent { f $\mathbf{3P_2}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$3P_2$. As the $C$-type vertices and $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, one edge of~$H$ must consist of two $k$-type vertices. This is not possible, as $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $3P_2$-free. \medskip
